title: Beginner Chess Course
description: Board setup, square names, piece movement, and the first rules every beginner needs.

categories.title: Rules of the Game
categories.description: Learn how the board works, how turns work, and how a chess game ends.

lessons.title: Name Every Square
lessons.summary: Use files and ranks to identify squares like d4, e5, and h8.
lessons.coachIntro: A chess coach always starts with the map. If you can name squares, every later lesson becomes easier.

steps.title: Meet the d-file and rank 4
steps.body: Watch the board light up. The d-file runs vertically, and rank 4 runs horizontally. Their intersection is d4.

steps.title: Find the d-file
steps.body: Click every square on the d-file.
steps.successText: Nice. You found the entire d-file.

steps.title: Find rank 4
steps.body: Now click every square on rank 4.
steps.successText: Great. You found rank 4.

steps.title: Find d4
steps.body: Click the square where file d and rank 4 meet.
steps.successText: Great. d4 is the intersection of the d-file and rank 4.

exercise.prompt: Finish by clicking d4 one more time.

lessons.title: Checkmate vs Stalemate
lessons.summary: Understand the difference between a forced win and a drawn position.
lessons.coachIntro: Beginners often mix up checkmate and stalemate. This lesson gives you a simple ending checklist.

steps.title: Know the difference
steps.body: Checkmate means the king is attacked and has no escape. Stalemate means the king is not attacked, but has no legal move.

steps.title: Is this checkmate or stalemate?
steps.body: Look at the board and choose the correct ending.
steps.successText: Correct. The king is attacked and has no escape.
steps.errorText: Not quite. This one is checkmate.

steps.title: Now spot the stalemate
steps.body: This one is different. The king is not in check, but still cannot move.
steps.successText: Correct. The king is stuck, but not in check.
steps.errorText: Not quite. This one is stalemate.

steps.title: Remember the difference
steps.body: Checkmate ends the game because the king is attacked. Stalemate ends the game because the king has no move.

categories.title: Piece Movement
categories.description: Practice how each piece moves and captures.

lessons.title: Move the Rook from d4
lessons.summary: Move the rook horizontally or vertically and avoid diagonal moves.
lessons.coachIntro: Rooks are powerful because they control long straight lines. You will see the legal squares, move the rook, then capture a target.

steps.title: Rooks travel on ranks and files
steps.body: The highlighted squares show every legal rook move from d4.

steps.title: Try a rook move
steps.body: Move the rook to any highlighted square from d4.
steps.successText: Nice. That is how a rook travels across a rank or file.

steps.title: Capture the hanging pawn
steps.body: Now capture the loose pawn on d7. The rook must move straight up the d-file.
steps.successText: Excellent. You used the rook's file to capture the hanging pawn.

exercise.prompt: Choose a destination square for the rook. The backend validates the move with python-chess.

lessons.title: Bishop Movement
lessons.summary: Learn how bishops travel diagonally and stay on one color.
lessons.coachIntro: Bishops and knights are both minor pieces, but their movement shapes are completely different.

steps.title: Bishops stay on diagonals
steps.body: The bishop can only move along diagonal lines, and it stays on the same color square.

steps.title: Move the bishop
steps.body: Pick any highlighted diagonal square from d4.
steps.successText: Nice. The bishop moved diagonally.

steps.title: Capture on the diagonal
steps.body: Now take the pawn on g7 with a diagonal bishop capture.
steps.successText: Correct. Bishops capture on diagonals.

exercise.prompt: Bishops stay on the same color. Is that true?

lessons.title: Knight Movement
lessons.summary: Practice the knight's L-shaped jump.
lessons.coachIntro: Knights feel strange at first because they are the only pieces that jump.

steps.title: Knights jump in an L
steps.body: The highlighted squares show every legal knight landing square. Nearby pieces do not stop the knight.

steps.title: Jump and capture
steps.body: Capture the pawn on f5 with a knight jump.
steps.successText: Nice. The knight jumped over the bishop and captured the pawn.

steps.title: Why did that work?
steps.body: Choose the reason the knight could make that move.
steps.successText: Exactly. Knights are the only pieces that jump over others.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The knight jumps independently.

exercise.prompt: Make another knight jump if you want to review.

lessons.title: Queen Movement
lessons.summary: Combine rook lines and bishop diagonals.
lessons.coachIntro: The queen is powerful because she combines straight and diagonal movement.

steps.title: Queen combines two patterns
steps.body: The queen moves like a rook and a bishop at the same time.

steps.title: Move like a rook
steps.body: Capture the pawn on d7 along the file.
steps.successText: Correct. The queen can move like a rook.

steps.title: Move like a bishop
steps.body: Now capture the pawn on g7 along the diagonal.
steps.successText: Correct. The queen can also move like a bishop.

exercise.prompt: The queen combines which two movement patterns?

lessons.title: King Movement
lessons.summary: Move the king safely one square at a time.
lessons.coachIntro: The king is slow, but every move matters because the king can never move into check.

steps.title: Kings move one square
steps.body: Green squares are safe. Red squares are attacked and not allowed.

steps.title: Move the king safely
steps.body: Choose a safe adjacent square for the king on e4.
steps.successText: Good. The king moved one square and stayed safe.

steps.title: Can the king move into check?
steps.body: Choose the correct rule.

choices.label: Yes, if the square is empty
No, the king must stay safe

steps.successText: Correct. The king can never move into check.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Empty is not enough if the square is attacked.

exercise.prompt: Find one more safe king move.

lessons.title: Pawn Movement
lessons.summary: Learn pawn moves, captures, first moves, and promotion.
lessons.coachIntro: Pawns look simple, but their movement rules create many beginner mistakes.

steps.title: Pawns move forward
steps.body: White pawns move up the board. Black pawns move down the board.

steps.title: Push the pawn
steps.body: Move the pawn one or two squares forward if the path is clear.
steps.successText: Good. Pawns move forward like that.

steps.title: Capture diagonally
steps.body: Pawns capture on the diagonals, not straight ahead.
steps.successText: Correct. Pawns capture diagonally.

steps.title: Promotion preview
steps.body: When a pawn reaches the last rank, it promotes.
steps.successText: Great. That pawn promoted on the last rank.

exercise.prompt: Capture diagonally or try the promotion preview again.

title: Opening Principles
description: Control the center, develop pieces, castle early, and avoid queen adventures.

categories.title: Basic Opening Principles
categories.description: Build good habits in the first few moves of the game.

lessons.title: Control the Center
lessons.summary: Play opening moves that fight for the middle of the board.
lessons.coachIntro: The center gives your pieces room to move and makes your position easier to develop.

steps.title: The center is the main battlefield
steps.body: The four center squares are the first squares beginners should learn to fight for.

steps.title: Play for the center
steps.body: Choose a good first move that helps control the middle.
steps.successText: Good. That move helps fight for the center or develop a piece.

steps.title: What are the center squares?
steps.body: Choose the four squares beginners watch first.
steps.successText: Exactly. Those four squares matter most at the start.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The center squares are d4, e4, d5, and e5.

lessons.title: Develop Your Pieces
lessons.summary: Bring knights and bishops into the game instead of moving the same pawn again and again.
lessons.coachIntro: Development means getting your pieces out where they can actually help.

steps.title: Minor pieces want to join the game
steps.body: Knights and bishops usually come out early so they can help attack the center.

steps.title: Develop a knight
steps.body: Move one of your knights toward the center.
steps.successText: Nice. That piece is now helping the position.

steps.title: What is development for?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: Leaving pieces on the back rank all game

steps.successText: Right. Development gets your pieces working together.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Pieces need active squares early on.

lessons.title: Castle Early
lessons.summary: Put the king in safety and connect your rook to the game.
lessons.coachIntro: Castling is usually the fastest way to make the king safer in the opening.

steps.title: King safety first
steps.body: Here the king can still castle because the path is clear.

steps.title: Castle kingside
steps.body: Move the king to the castled square.
steps.successText: Good. The king is safer and the rook joins the game.

steps.title: Why castle?
steps.body: Choose the best reason.

choices.label: To move the queen for free

steps.successText: Exactly. Castling improves king safety and rook activity.
steps.errorText: Not quite. King safety is the main reason.

lessons.title: Do Not Move the Queen Too Early
lessons.summary: Learn why bringing the queen out too soon usually loses time.
lessons.coachIntro: A queen move can look active, but beginners often lose time by moving it too early.

steps.title: The queen can become a target
steps.body: If the queen leaves too early, the opponent can gain time by chasing it around.

steps.title: Which move is usually too early?
steps.body: Pick the queen move beginners should avoid at the start.
steps.successText: Correct. Early queen adventures usually waste time.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The queen move is the risky one here.

steps.title: What should usually come first?
steps.body: Choose the better opening habit.
steps.successText: Yes. Development and king safety come first.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The queen is usually not the first job.

lessons.title: Connect Your Rooks
lessons.summary: Free the back rank so your rooks can support each other.
lessons.coachIntro: Once the queen and minor pieces move out, the rooks can start working together.

steps.title: Rooks like open lines
steps.body: Connected rooks are a sign that the opening is going well.

steps.title: What helps the rooks connect?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.
steps.successText: Right. Rooks connect when the pieces between them move out of the way.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Development is what opens the rooks up.

steps.title: What is a bad early habit?
steps.body: Pick the choice that usually slows development.

choices.label: Moving the same piece again and again

steps.successText: Exactly. Wasting tempos slows the opening down.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Repeating the same piece is usually the mistake.

title: Blunder Checks
description: Pause before moving and scan for hanging pieces, checks, captures, and threats.

categories.title: Blunder Checks
categories.description: Pause before moving so you do not give away pieces for free.

lessons.title: Checks, Captures, Threats
lessons.summary: Use a quick scan before every move.
lessons.coachIntro: Most beginner games are decided by one-move mistakes. A short safety scan prevents many of them.

steps.title: A hanging piece
steps.body: A hanging piece is attacked and not ready to be saved.

steps.title: Click the hanging piece
steps.body: Which piece is hanging here?
steps.successText: Correct. The knight on c3 is hanging.

steps.title: Save the knight
steps.body: Move the knight to a safer square.
steps.successText: Nice. You moved the knight out of danger.

exercise.prompt: Point to the hanging knight once more.

title: Basic Tactics
description: Forks, pins, skewers, discovered attacks, hanging pieces, and removing the defender.

categories.title: Basic Tactics
categories.description: Recognize simple patterns that win material or create checkmate threats.

lessons.title: Spot the Fork Idea
lessons.summary: A fork attacks two valuable targets at the same time.
lessons.coachIntro: Tactics are patterns. You do not need magic vision, just a repeatable way to search.

steps.title: A fork hits two targets
steps.body: One knight move can attack the king and queen at the same time.

steps.title: Find the fork move
steps.body: Move the knight to the square that attacks both targets.
steps.successText: Nice. That's the kind of move that creates a fork.

steps.title: Why is a fork strong?
steps.body: Choose the best explanation.

choices.label: It attacks two targets at once

steps.successText: Exactly. The opponent usually cannot save both pieces.
steps.errorText: Not quite. A fork works because it hits two targets at once.

exercise.prompt: Try to make the fork move on the board.

lessons.title: Pins
lessons.summary: A pinned piece cannot move because it would expose something more valuable.
lessons.coachIntro: Pins are simple. Find the piece that is stuck in front of a more valuable target.

steps.title: A piece gets pinned
steps.body: The bishop lines up the knight with the king.

steps.title: Pin the knight
steps.body: Move the bishop to the square that creates the pin.
steps.successText: Nice. The knight is pinned to the king.

steps.title: Why is the knight stuck?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: Moving it would expose the king
It is blocked by a rook

steps.successText: Exactly. A pinned piece cannot move freely.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The king is the important piece behind it.

lessons.title: Skewers
lessons.summary: A skewer attacks the most valuable piece first and reveals a more valuable piece behind it.
lessons.coachIntro: A skewer is like a pin in reverse. The stronger piece gets chased away and the weaker one falls behind it.

steps.title: The king is in front of the queen
steps.body: If the king moves, the queen behind it becomes vulnerable.

steps.title: Skewer the queen behind the king
steps.body: Move the rook to the checking square on the file.
steps.successText: Good. The king is forced to move and the queen is left exposed.

steps.title: What happens after the king moves?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: The queen behind it becomes the target

steps.successText: Right. The weak piece behind the king becomes the target.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The whole point is to expose the queen behind the king.

lessons.title: Discovered Attacks
lessons.summary: Move one piece and reveal an attack from another piece behind it.
lessons.coachIntro: The hidden piece matters. When it finally gets to see the line, it can create a big tactic.

steps.title: One move reveals another attack
steps.body: The bishop is blocking the rook. Move it away and the rook suddenly attacks the king.

steps.title: Reveal the attack
steps.body: Move the bishop to open the rook’s line.
steps.successText: Excellent. The rook now attacks the king along the file.

steps.title: What is a discovered attack?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: A hidden piece attacks after another piece moves away
A piece that only attacks diagonally

steps.successText: Yes. One piece moves and another piece becomes active behind it.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The attack is revealed by moving the front piece.

lessons.title: Removing the Defender
lessons.summary: Capture the piece that is defending something more important.
lessons.coachIntro: If a piece is defending the real target, sometimes the first job is to remove that defender.

steps.title: Find the defender
steps.body: The knight protects the queen, but it can be taken.

steps.title: Remove the defender
steps.body: Capture the knight that is guarding the queen.
steps.successText: Great. The defender is gone and the queen becomes vulnerable.

steps.title: Why was that good?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: The queen behind it is now attacked
The bishop is now trapped forever

steps.successText: Exactly. Removing the defender exposes the real target.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The queen was the real target all along.

lessons.title: Hanging Pieces
lessons.summary: Spot loose material and win it right away.
lessons.coachIntro: A hanging piece is simply a piece that is attacked and not protected well enough.

steps.title: Spot the loose queen
steps.body: The queen on d4 is hanging and can be won immediately.

steps.title: Win the hanging queen
steps.body: Capture the loose queen with the rook.
steps.successText: Nice. You spotted the hanging piece and won it immediately.

steps.title: What is a hanging piece?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: A piece that is attacked and poorly defended
A piece that can only move backward

steps.successText: Exactly. Hanging pieces are loose material waiting to be taken.
steps.errorText: Not quite. A hanging piece is just a loose piece.

title: Checkmate Patterns
description: Mate in 1, back-rank mates, queen-and-king mates, ladder mates, and smothered mate ideas.

categories.title: Checkmate Patterns
categories.description: Learn the simplest mating nets, from mate in 1 to classic beginner checkmates.

lessons.title: Find Mate in 1
lessons.summary: Spot a simple mating net and finish with one move.
lessons.coachIntro: Mate in 1 puzzles are about forcing moves. The king should feel boxed in before you even move.

steps.title: The king has no room
steps.body: The queen and king work together to trap the black king in the corner.

steps.title: Play the mate
steps.body: Move the queen to the square that finishes the game.
steps.successText: Correct. The queen lands on g7 and the king has no escape.

steps.title: Why is this mate?
steps.body: Choose the best reason.

choices.label: The king has no legal squares

steps.successText: Exactly. A checkmate works because the king cannot run or capture safely.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The key is that the king has no legal escape.

lessons.title: Back-Rank Mate
lessons.summary: Use the back rank when the enemy king is trapped by its own pawns.
lessons.coachIntro: Back-rank mates happen when the king cannot flee because its own pawns block the way.

steps.title: The back rank is crowded
steps.body: The black king is stuck behind its own pawns.

steps.title: Deliver the back-rank mate
steps.body: Move the rook to the checking square on the eighth rank.
steps.successText: Nice. The rook lands on e8 and the king is checkmated.

steps.title: What made this mate possible?
steps.body: Choose the best reason.

choices.label: The king had no air on the back rank
The queen was worth less than the rook

steps.successText: Right. The king was trapped behind its own pawns.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The problem is that the king cannot step off the back rank.

lessons.title: Ladder Mate Basics
lessons.summary: Use a rook to drive the king toward the edge.
lessons.coachIntro: Ladder mate is a pattern of repeated checks that push the king to the edge of the board.

steps.title: Drive the king upward
steps.body: The rook can swing over to the seventh rank and keep the king boxed in.

steps.title: Take the seventh rank
steps.body: Capture the pawn and give the first checking rook move.
steps.successText: Good. The rook takes the seventh rank and starts the ladder.

steps.title: What is the idea here?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: Keep checking and push the king toward the edge
Trade the rook for a pawn

steps.successText: Exactly. Ladder mate is about repeated checks and king confinement.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The goal is to keep driving the king back.

lessons.title: Queen and King Mate
lessons.summary: Bring your king close so the queen can finish the job.
lessons.coachIntro: When your king joins the attack, the queen can often deliver a clean mate in the corner.

steps.title: The queen is supported
steps.body: The king helps protect the queen on the mating square.

steps.title: Finish the king and queen mate
steps.body: Play the queen move that wins the game.
steps.successText: Excellent. The queen lands on g7 and the king is trapped.

steps.title: Why is the queen safe?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.
steps.successText: Right. The king protects the queen from being taken.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The king is the key helper here.

lessons.title: Smothered Mate Intro
lessons.summary: See how a knight can deliver mate when the king is boxed in by its own pieces.
lessons.coachIntro: A smothered mate happens when the king is stuck behind its own pieces and a knight jumps in with the final blow.

steps.title: The king is smothered
steps.body: The black pieces are doing the defending for White by accident.

steps.title: Jump to the mating square
steps.body: Move the knight to the square that finishes the smothered mate.
steps.successText: Great. The knight jumps in and the king has nowhere to go.

steps.title: What makes it smothered?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: The king is blocked by its own pieces
The knight moves like a bishop

steps.successText: Exactly. The king cannot escape because its own pieces are in the way.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The king is trapped by its own army.

title: Endgame Basics
description: King activity, promotion, opposition, passed pawns, and basic winning technique.

categories.title: Endgame Basics
categories.description: Learn king activity, pawn promotion, opposition, and simple winning technique.

lessons.title: Learn Opposition
lessons.summary: Take the key square so your king can outmaneuver the enemy king.
lessons.coachIntro: Opposition is a king-vs-king idea where the side to move can force progress.

steps.title: The kings face each other
steps.body: Opposition matters when the kings are on the same file or rank with one square between them.

steps.title: Take the opposition
steps.body: Move the white king to the square that faces the black king directly.
steps.successText: Nice. You took the key square in front of the black king.

steps.title: What does opposition do?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: Helps the king gain a key square
Moves the queen to the side

steps.successText: Exactly. Opposition helps your king make progress.
steps.errorText: Not quite. It is a king maneuver idea.

lessons.title: King Activity Matters
lessons.summary: In the endgame, the king becomes a strong fighting piece.
lessons.coachIntro: The king is weak in the opening but strong in the endgame. This lesson teaches that switch.

steps.title: The king should move forward
steps.body: Bring the king toward the center where it can help the pawn.

steps.title: Centralize the king
steps.body: Move the white king toward the middle of the board.
steps.successText: Good. The king is moving toward the action.

steps.title: Why is king activity important?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: The king can help win pawns
The king must stay in the corner forever

steps.successText: Right. In the endgame, the king is part of the attack.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Endgame kings are active pieces.

lessons.title: Pawn Promotion
lessons.summary: Push a pawn to the last rank and turn it into a queen.
lessons.coachIntro: Promotion is one of the most exciting endgame goals, and beginners should recognize it early.

steps.title: One step from glory
steps.body: A pawn that reaches the last rank promotes.

steps.title: Promote the pawn
steps.body: Move the pawn to the last rank and choose a queen.
steps.successText: Great. The pawn promotes to a queen on the last rank.

steps.title: What can a promoted pawn become?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: A queen, rook, bishop, or knight

steps.successText: Exactly. A pawn can promote into any major piece except a king.
steps.errorText: Not quite. Promotion gives you a new piece choice.

lessons.title: Passed Pawns and King Support
lessons.summary: Escort a passed pawn with your king so it can march forward safely.
lessons.coachIntro: A passed pawn becomes dangerous when your king is nearby and the enemy king is too far away.

steps.title: Support the pawn
steps.body: Your king should walk in front of the pawn or beside it to help it advance.

steps.title: Escort the pawn
steps.body: Move the king closer so it can support the pawn.
steps.successText: Nice. The king steps in to support the passed pawn.

steps.title: What helps a passed pawn most?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.
steps.successText: Right. King support makes passed pawns much stronger.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The king is the key helper here.

lessons.title: Basic Rook Mate Technique
lessons.summary: Use a rook with your king to finish a simple endgame mate.
lessons.coachIntro: Rook mates are one of the most useful basic endgame skills for beginners.

steps.title: The rook takes the eighth rank
steps.body: The rook and queen work together to trap the king on the back rank.

steps.title: Deliver the rook mate
steps.body: Move the rook to the mating square.
steps.successText: Excellent. The rook lands on e8 and the king is checkmated.

steps.title: What matters in this mate?
steps.body: Choose the best answer.

choices.label: The king cannot escape the back rank
The rook is always stronger than the queen

steps.successText: Exactly. The rook works because the king has no escape squares.
steps.errorText: Not quite. The king is trapped behind its own pawns.
